analysis:
Both changed files are CI test scripts: scripts/test-darkbloom-route.py and scripts/test-provider-ci-workflow.py. They add no runtime provider, coordinator or attestation code. The PR changes test expectations so each test-provider matrix shard reads its own route lane (`test-provider-<shard>`), with a per-lane count of 1 in place of a single lane of count 5. The new helpers `matrix_shards`, `job_lanes`, `requested_lanes` and `SHARDED` (head lines 69-71, 129-142) derive the expected lanes. `test_routed_jobs_read_their_lane_and_keep_their_fallback` (head 488-522) and `test_route_requests_exactly_one_lane_per_provider_shard` in the provider CI test enforce this layout.

Security-relevant controls kept or reinforced by the tests:
- Exact label-array matching, so only the exact Darkbloom label array is accepted from the plane.
- Fallback to the Blacksmith runner on any plane failure.
- HTTPS-only plane contact with certificate verification kept on.
- Fork pull requests never contact the plane.
- Route-step injection hardening.
- Routed jobs limited to read-only permissions, no `id-token`, no secrets, and a timeout of 60 minutes or less.
- Release and credentialed workflows (UNROUTED) kept on literal Blacksmith runners, with no self-hosted labels.

Per-shard lanes affect only which runner is granted. They do not widen privilege. A plane that grants some shards and not others yields mixed runners, but each shard still gets either an exact label array or its fallback. The test-side parsing is regex-based and could miss unusual YAML. That is a test-fidelity limit, not a security regression.

I found no impact on the provider threat model assets or boundaries (TB-002, TB-011, A-001 and the rest). The actual darkbloom-route.yml, ci.yml and plane-side behaviour were not supplied, so I could not check that the workflows match the new test expectations.
